name: William Parker
bio: A groom, brother of Charles Parker, present at the pick-up in the St James's Restaurant bar and at the Rupert Street dinner where Wilde fed Charles from his own fork and spoon and passed him a preserved cherry mouth-to-mouth. He understood from the outset that the brothers 'were to be treated as women, and that you were to have money for it'; he went twice to Little College Street, shared Taylor's bed with his brother one night — his testimony describes an attempted sodomy by Taylor — then took country work as a groom and 'had nothing more to do with Taylor or with Mr. Wilde.' Taylor was convicted of gross indecency with him (count 9) on 21 May 1895.
bio_sources: William Parker's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 198-199
Verdict at Taylor's trial, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 292
Taylor's account of the brothers staying a week, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 284
bio_note: Taylor said he ultimately 'persuaded William Parker to go home to his father' (p. 284). Dates: not found. Unlike his brother Charles, William gave no age on oath in the Hyde text: his examination-in-chief opens with his occupation, 'I have been employed as a groom'. McKenna, Secret Life (2008), p. 341, reports only Taylor's guess that the two brothers 'were sixteen or seventeen, or thereabouts' when he met them - a bystander's estimate of two people at once, not an age statement, and nothing is inferred from it. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.
